presenceLabel: Illinois (Illiniwek) town or declared claim in this area
presenceNote: The story is an event of 1778 (two town points, no boundary). The 1803 claim is the one sourced boundary: the Kaskaskia declared it for the confederacy, and the Ohio and Mississippi reaches can be placed (medium confidence for the river calls). The inland calls follow unlocated ridges (low confidence), so the inland edge of the tint is a rough guess. The claim’s southern edge is the Ohio River; no Kentucky territory is shown. The page spans 1778–1803 to include the 1803 claim.
overlapNote: Piankashaw (Wabash side: the 1804 treaty Art. 2 acknowledges the Kaskaskia right to sell their ceded country, separated from Piankashaw land by the Wabash/Saline Creek and Wabash/Mississippi-tributary divides), Kickapoo (took part of Illinois 'by conquest from the Illinois nation', 1819 treaty), Potawatomi and Miami to the north and east. Shawnee and Cherokee Kentucky claims do not overlap (west bank of the claim is the Ohio).
basis: Kaskaskia treaty 1803 (text), Piankeshaw treaty 1804 Art. 2, NPS Clark NHP page, Wikipedia coordinates for the towns.

eras.label: July–Sept 1778 · Clark at Cahokia and Kaskaskia
eras.text: Clark took Kaskaskia, Prairie du Rocher and Cahokia in July 1778, then held a council at Cahokia in late summer with leaders of nearby tribes; many accepted the white belt of peace, many others stayed allied with the British (NPS). The two towns are approximate points, and the tint is an approximate general area of the Illinois towns on the Mississippi bottom, built from whole counties.

eras.label: 1803 · The claim the Kaskaskia declared
eras.text: On 13 Aug 1803 at Vincennes the Kaskaskia, who spoke for all the Illinois tribes (Kaskaskia, Michigamea, Cahokia and Tamaroa, ‘reduced to a very small number’), ceded their Illinois lands, reserving about 350 acres near Kaskaskia. Their declared claim begins at the Ohio–Mississippi mouth and runs up the Ohio to Saline Creek, about twelve miles below the mouth of the Wabash, then along ridges between the Wabash and Kaskaskia waters to the Illinois River and down to its mouth, then down the Mississippi. The southern edge is the Ohio River itself: nothing south of the river is claimed, so no Kentucky county is inside it. The darker counties touch the Ohio (river call); the lighter tint is a rough guess at the inland area, because the ridge calls are not located. Saline Creek is not placed on this map.
